Photoredox-Catalyzed α‑Aminoalkylcarboxylation of Allenes with
CO2
Hyungwoo Hahm, Doohyun Baek, Dowon Kim, Seongwook Park, Jeong Yup Ryoo, and Sukwon Hong *
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2021, 23, 3879 −3884 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: The photoredox-catalyzed α-aminoalkylcarboxylation of aryl
allenes with CO 2 and N,N-dimethylanilines is reported for the ﬁrst time (26
examples, up to 96% yield). In the case of electron-de ﬁcient allenes, good
regioselectivity was observed (up to 94:6), exclusively generating kinetic
products over thermodynamic products. This protocol is a novel synthetic
method for highly functionalized β,γ-unsaturated γ-aminobutyric esters.
γ-Aminobutyric acid is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in
the mammalian central nervous system.
1 For this reason, the
synthesis of structurally diverse γ-aminobutyric acid derivatives
has been considered important in the pharmaceutical ﬁeld.2 In
particular, various γ-aminobutyric acids bearing a tertiary
carbon center at the β-position such as pregabalin, 3 baclofen,4
phenibut,5 and rolipram6 have been investigated ( Figure 1). In
this regard, more structurally diverse, β-substituted γ-amino-
butyric acid derivatives have been developed to expand the
potential bioactive pharmaceutical library.
7
Typical approaches have been developed through the
Michael addition of carbonyl compounds to β-substituted
nitroalkenes or the conjugate addition of nitromethane to α,β-
unsaturated aldehydes. 7a−d Another approach involves the
photocatalytic radical conjugate addition of α,β-unsaturated
compounds to amines. 7e−i Recently, the visible-light-mediated
difunctionalization of alkenes with CO 2 and various radical
sources to obtain valuable carboxylic acids has received
increasing attention.
8
Among the developed methods, the photoredox-catalyzed α-
aminoalkylcarboxylation of electron-deﬁcient alkenes with CO 2
in the presence of 1,2,3,5-tetrakis(carbazol-9-yl)-4,6-dicyano-
benzene (4CzIPN) for γ-aminobutyric acid synthesis was
independently developed by Wu and Xi ( Scheme 1a).8c,e Very
recently, the photoredox-catalyzed α-aminoalkylcarboxylation
of activated alkenes with α-amino acids as a bifunctional
reagent for γ-aminobutyric acid synthesis was reported by Yu
and Cheng and Sun ( Scheme 1 a).8a,h However, β-substituted
γ-aminobutyric acid synthesis with CO 2 remains a great
challenge due to the utilization of β-substituted alkenes with
high reduction potential. 9 We envisioned that the photo-
catalytic α-aminoalkylcarboxylation of allenes with CO 2 and
amines would serve as an ideal approach to deliver a novel γ-
aminobutyric acid through the incorporation of the ethylene
moiety at the β-position. Allenes, as special and versatile
synthons with structural diversity, have received much
attention in organic chemistry.
10
Although various allene difunctionalization methods have
been investigated, few studies have been developed on the
transition-metal-catalyzed difunctionalization of allenes with
CO2 for unsaturated carboxylic acid derivatives. 11 To the best
of our knowledge, there have been no examples demonstrating
the photocatalytic difunctionalization of allenes with CO 2 in a
redox-neutral fashion. Herein we report the visible-light-
mediated α-aminoalkylcarboxylation of aryl allenes with CO
2

and amines for β,γ-unsaturated γ-aminobutyric ester synthesis
(Scheme 1 b). This reaction is the ﬁrst example of the
photoredox-catalyzed difunctionalization of aryl allenes with
CO
2. Compared with the photocatalytic difunctionalization of
alkenes with CO 2,8 the photocatalytic difunctionalization of
allenes with CO 2 is more challenging due to their
regioselectivity control issues. 10,11 A previous report indicated
that the combination of a photocatalyst and base was
important for regioselective radical addition to 2,3-allenoates.
12
Encouraged by this result, we initially investigated the reaction
by using 4-tri ﬂuoromethylphenylallene 1a as a model substrate
with N,N-4-trimethylaniline 2a as a radical source in the
presence of 1 mol % Ir(dF(CF
3)ppy)2(dtbpy)·PF6 when using
1-methyl-2-pyrrolidinone (NMP) and a base under 15 W blue
light-emitting diode (LED) irradiation at room temperature
with CO
2 at atmospheric pressure ( Table 1). We examined the
reaction with bases such as CsOH ·H2O, NaOAc, and K 2HPO4
(Table 1, entries 1−3). In base screening, K 2HPO4 showed the
best regioselectivity compared with other bases, although the
yield slightly decreased. Next, we tested some other photo-
catalysts. Ir(dF(CF
3)ppy)2(bpy)·PF6, Ir(ppy) 2(bpy)·PF6, Ir-
(ppy) 3, 1,2,3,5-tetrakis(carbazol -9-yl)-4,6-dicyanobenzene
(4CzIPN), and (2,3,4,6)-3-benzyl-2,4,5,6-tetra(9 H-carbazol-
9yl)benzonitrile (4CzBnBN) gave relatively low regioselectiv-
ities and yields ( Table 1 , entries 4 −8). To improve the
selectivity of the kinetic product 3aa, the reaction must
proceed at a low temperature. By reacting at 0 °C, the
selectivity and yield increased ( Table 1, entry 9). We observed
that the selectivity signi ﬁcantly increased while reacting at −20
°C, but the yield decreased ( Table 1 , entry 10). In addition,
some other solvents were investigated. N,N-dimethylforma-
mide (DMF) and N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMA) were both
eﬃcient in terms of the yield and selectivity ( Table 1 , entries
11 and 12). Finally, no traces of the desired products were
detected in the absence of the photocatalyst or light ( Table 1 ,
entries 13 and 14).
With these optimized reaction conditions in hand, the
aniline substrate scope of α-aminoalkylcarboxylation with 1a
was examined ( Scheme 2 ). Compared with para-methyl-

substituted N,N-dimethylaniline ( 2a), meta-methyl-substituted
N,N-dimethylanilines ( 2b,c) gave higher yields of the desired
products, but the regioselectivity slightly decreased ( 3/4aa−
ac). The non- ( 2d), bromo- ( 2e), chloro- ( 2f), ﬂuoro- ( 2g),
and methoxy- ( 2h) substituted N,N-dimethylanilines at the
para position of the phenyl ring have an excellent yield and
moderate regioselectivity, except for 4-methoxy- N,N-dimethy-
laniline ( 3/4ad−ah). Other heteroaryl amines, such as
pyridine and quinoline, successfully gave moderate yields of
the desired products ( 3/4ai−aj). Notably, the utilization of
secondary amines and tertiary amines such as 4-dimethylami-
nopyridine (DMAP), N,N-dimehtylthiophene-3-amine, potas-
sium (4-methylphenoxy)carbonylaminomethyltri ﬂuoroborate,
and tert-butyl methyl( p-tolyl)carbamate, did not lead to the
desired products.
13 (See Scheme S1 in the Supporting
Information.)
Next, the reaction scope was studied with aryl allenes 1 and
2a (Scheme 3 ). Hammett σm/p values could be in accord with
the selectivity of compounds 3 and 4 under the applied
reaction conditions. 14 Electron-deﬁcient phenylallenes with
positive σ values undergo regioselective α-aminoalkylcarbox-
ylation regardless of the substitution pattern. Phenylallenes
bearing highly electron-withdrawing groups such as tri ﬂuor-
omethyl (1b), cyano ( 1c), keto carbonyl ( 1d), or ester groups
(1e) at the para or meta position in the benzene ring were
eﬀective at giving the desired kinetic products in good yield
with good regioselectivity ( 3/4ba−3/4ea). The introduction
of weakly electron-withdrawing substituents, such as chloro
(1f−h), bromo ( 1i−j), and ﬂuoro (1k−l) groups at the ortho,
meta, or para position of the phenyl ring, gave moderate to
good yields and regioselectivity, except for 4- ﬂuoro-phenyl-
allene ( 3/4fa−la). Phenylallene ( 1m)a n dp h e n y l a l l e n e -
bearing methoxy groups ( 1n−o) at the meta or para position
of the phenyl ring exhibited poor regioselectivity ( 3/4ma−oa).
Electron-neutral and electron-donating-group-substituted ben-
zyl radicals with high reduction potentials ( −1.43 V vs
standard calomel electrode (SCE) for the H benzyl radical
analog and −1.75 V vs SCE for the p-OMe benzyl radical
analog) were di ﬃcult to reduce by Ir(dF(CF
3)ppy)2(dtbpy)·
PF6 ((E1/2Ir(II)/Ir(III)) = −1.37 V vs SCE in MeCN). 9,15a
Fortunately, it is presumed that allenes are easily reduced via
an allyl-benzyl anion intermediate. When using 1,1-diaryl-
substituted allenes at room temperature, a thermodynamically
favorable product was obtained in moderate yield with
excellent regioselectivity ( 4pa−qa). The electron density and

structure of aryl allenes have a strong e ﬀect on the
regioselectivity. Unfortunately, the utilization of ethyl-2,3-
butadienoate did not lead to the desired products. (See
Scheme S1 in the Supporting Information .)
To gain insight into the e ﬃciency of the α-amino-
alkylcarboxylation of allenes with CO
2, preliminary mecha-
nistic experiments were conducted ( Scheme 4 ). Continuous-
light irradiation was an essential factor preventing hydro-
aminoalkylation.8c Stern−Volmer luminescence studies con-
ﬁrm that the light-activated Ir photocatalyst (( E1/2Ir(III)*/
Ir(II)) = +1.21 V vs SCE in MeCN) 15 was quenched by 2a
(Eoxp = +0.74 V vs SCE) rather than 1a (Scheme 4; see Figures
S1 and S2 in the Supporting Information ). When the radical
scavenger 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperdinyloxyl (TEMPO) was
used as an additive in the α-aminoalkylcarboxylation, the
desired products were not observed. The radical adduct was
detected by high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS)
(Scheme 4 and Figure S3 in the Supporting Information ).
This result indicates that α-aminoalkylcarboxylation might rely
on the radical pathway. The isotope-labeling experiments with
D
2O instead of CO 2 showed that benzyl allyl anion species
were present in the catalytic cycle ( Scheme 4; see Figure S4 in
the Supporting Information ).
On the basis of the experimental results and the related refs
10, 12, and 16, the proposed mechanism of the regioselective
α-aminoalkylcarboxylation to aryl allenes is outlined in Scheme
5. The α-aminomethyl radical ( 2′′), which is produced by a
photoexcited photocatalyst and base, undergoes addition to the
central carbon of the allenes ( 1a) to give a radical delocalized
intermediate (A). A subsequent single-electron transfer (SET)
between A and the reduced photocatalyst Ir(II) gives the
delocalized allyl-benzyl carbanion. The carbanion intermedi-
ates ( B) attack CO
2 as nucleophiles, a ﬀording the expected
β,γ-unsaturated γ-aminobutyric esters (3a) after treatment with
TMSCHN2. The photocatalyst was regenerated by SET in the
catalytic cycle. A gram-scale reaction was readily conducted.
(See Scheme S4 in the Supporting Information .) To
demonstrate the utility of this reaction, the unsaturated γ-
aminobutyric ester 3aa was reduced by lithium aluminum
hydride (LAH) to form δ-amino alcohol 6. (See Scheme S5 in
the Supporting Information .)
In summary, we demonstrated the photoredox-catalyzed
intermolecular α-aminoalkylcarboxylation of aryl allenes with
CO
2 and amines in a redox-neutral fashion for the ﬁrst time.
Twenty-six examples of various aryl allenes and amines were
demonstrated to a ﬀord good isolated yields (up to 96%).
Electron-deﬁcient substituted aryl allenes show great regiose-
lectivity. This sustainable process is the general synthetic
method of unsaturated γ-aminobutyric esters. α-Amino-
alkylcarboxylation has the advantages of step and atom
economy and mild conditions. The application and detailed
reaction mechanism are currently ongoing.
